whyCorrect: The text sets up a problem and then hands you the fix. The problem: reading the piece as being about constraints on women leaves Sandoval, a man taped to the same wall, unexplained. The fix is the 1974 context — the art establishment recognized only sociohistorical muralists, so every nonmuralist Chicano artist, male or female, was boxed in by aesthetic expectations. A conclusion that "accounts for all the evidence" has to cover both artists, and only the reading about Chicano artists in general does that.

whyWrong.A: Splits the work into two separate meanings, one per artist, when the text asks for a single interpretation that accounts for all the evidence; it also assigns frustration to muralists, who were the group the establishment did recognize.
whyWrong.B: Keeps women at the center, which is exactly the reading the text says fails because it cannot explain Sandoval.
whyWrong.C: Turns the muralists themselves into the target. The text criticizes the establishment for recognizing only muralists, never the content of what muralists depicted.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that sounds most sophisticated instead of the one that resolves the specific gap the text identifies.
tips: When a text names an unexplained detail, the correct completion is the one that explains that detail.

whyCorrect: Neither noun owns anything here. You place your hands (more than one hand, plain plural) between the two antennas (plain plural, and "two" already tells you it is plural). Nothing belongs to the hands and nothing belongs to the antennas, so no apostrophe is needed anywhere.

whyWrong.A: Uses the singular "hand's" after "your ... two antennas" implies both hands, and adds a possessive apostrophe to "antenna's" where the sentence needs the plain plural "antennas."
whyWrong.C: Marks both nouns as possessive. Ask what the hands own and what the antennas own — the sentence never says, which is the signal that no apostrophe belongs.
whyWrong.D: Correctly leaves "antennas" plain but still makes "hands'" possessive; the hands do not own the space between the antennas, they are simply placed there.

tips: Before writing an apostrophe, finish the phrase "the ___ of the ___." If it makes no sense, you need a plain plural.

whyCorrect: The blank sits inside a three-item list of past participles: the sculptures had been cut, bent, and welded. A list of three takes a comma after each of the first two items and nothing after the conjunction, so the punctuation you need is "cut, bent, and" followed directly by "welded."

whyWrong.A: Adds a comma after "and," which separates the conjunction from the item it introduces; nothing ever goes between "and" and the last list item.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon separates full clauses or items that already contain commas. "Cut" and "bent" are single words, so a semicolon is far too heavy here.
whyWrong.D: Drops the comma after "cut," leaving the first two items run together as "cut bent" instead of as separate list items.

tips: Count the list items first; three parallel items means two commas and no punctuation after the conjunction.

whyCorrect: Strip the modifier and the subject is plain: "the toxins ... increase its attractiveness." Everything between "toxins" and the blank — "the organism uses to protect itself from predation" — is a relative clause describing the toxins, not a new subject. A plural subject in the present tense takes the base form "increase."

whyWrong.A: "Is" agrees with a singular subject, and the progressive also implies an action in progress rather than the general fact the sentence states.
whyWrong.C: Singular verb form. It sounds right only if you let "predation" or "the organism," the nearest nouns to the blank, act as the subject.
whyWrong.D: Singular, and the present perfect frames this as something that has happened rather than as a standing property of the toxins.

commonMistakes: Agreeing the verb with whichever noun sits closest to the blank instead of with the real subject.

whyCorrect: Two things have to happen at the blank. "Respectively" belongs to the main sentence — it tells you which molar mass goes with which compound — so it stays outside the parentheses and is set off by a comma. Then the whole side note about stoichiometry opens with the parenthesis, giving "g/mol, respectively (in stoichiometry, molar mass helps convert ...)."

whyWrong.A: Pulls "respectively" inside the parentheses, so the main sentence loses the word that pairs each number with its compound and the aside becomes two unrelated statements jammed together.
whyWrong.B: Places a comma immediately before an opening parenthesis. Punctuation never goes directly in front of "("; if a mark is needed there, it goes after the closing parenthesis.
whyWrong.C: Ends the sentence at "g/mol" and starts a new one with "Respectively," which now modifies nothing, and it opens the parenthesis in the middle of the aside so the parenthetical no longer contains a complete thought.

tips: Decide what belongs inside the parentheses before you decide where the commas go.

whyCorrect: Test both sides of the blank on their own. "Cut, bent, and welded ... the sculptures ... are meant to challenge viewers to consider their own relationships to material wastes" is a complete sentence, and "her thought-provoking works in the 1999 exhibition ... were no different" is also a complete sentence. Two independent clauses joined with no coordinating conjunction require a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: "And to" tries to extend the earlier list, producing "relationships to material wastes and to her thought-provoking works ... were no different," which leaves the second clause with no grammatical home.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: No punctuation at all fuses the two clauses into a run-on.

commonMistakes: Assuming the second half continues the first because it starts with "her"; check whether it has its own subject and verb, and here it does.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is the gerund phrase "Distinguishing 'exactly the same' and 'nearly the same' commodities," and a gerund phrase is always singular no matter how many nouns sit inside it. The dashes fence off "whether crops, lumber, or precious metals" as an interruption, so it cannot supply the subject. Singular subject, past tense: "was."

whyWrong.A: Plural verb, chosen by agreeing with the plural nouns "commodities" or "metals" instead of with the gerund phrase that heads the subject.
whyWrong.C: "Having been" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence never gets a main verb and stays a fragment.
whyWrong.D: "Being" is likewise nonfinite and leaves the sentence with no predicate.

tips: Cross out anything between a pair of dashes before deciding what the subject is.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a claim — the upward trend in urbanization held "throughout that part of the continent" — and the second sentence backs it with the region-wide figures, 44.5% to 47.7% over the same years. That is confirmation of the claim just made, which is what "Indeed" signals.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" announces a contrast, but the regional numbers rise just as Burkina's do, so there is nothing to contrast.
whyWrong.B: "Later" marks a shift forward in time, yet both sentences cover the identical 2015-2020 window.
whyWrong.D: "In reality" corrects a mistaken impression; the second sentence confirms the first rather than correcting it.

commonMistakes: Reading two different sets of percentages as a contrast when they actually move in the same direction.

whyCorrect: The colon sets up what follows as the outcome of the plant pulling iron out of the ground and locking it into its roots and shoots. If the iron ends up inside the plant, the soil necessarily has less of it. The blank needs a cause-and-effect signal, and "accordingly" is the one that says "as a result of what was just described."

whyWrong.A: "Specifically" promises a narrower restatement of the previous idea, but soil concentrations dropping is a new consequence, not a detail of how the plant stores iron.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" sets up a contrast; falling soil iron agrees with the storage described before it, so there is nothing to contrast.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" makes the two facts parallel and independent, hiding the fact that one causes the other.

tips: Ask whether the second idea follows from the first or merely sits beside it; only the first case takes a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes when these amphibians migrate: during the day, unlike most animals. The second sentence explains what happens in that daytime window — the sun is up, so predators that hunt by sight can see the warning colors. The blank has to point back to that time period, which is what "At that time" does.

whyWrong.B: "For example" would require the second sentence to be an instance of the claim before it, but it gives the reason daytime migration is safe rather than an example of it.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, and the second sentence adds new information about color patterns and predator vision.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, yet the second sentence supports the first by explaining how the amphibians stay safe.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a contrast word because the first sentence starts with "While"; that contrast is already handled inside the sentence itself.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing: the role Morris played. His role is keyboardist, and the notes add that he was one of the musicians invited to tour. Choice A puts both in the predicate — "performed with OTS as a touring keyboardist" — so the sentence lands on what he did rather than on when he did it.

whyWrong.B: Uses Morris only as one end of a range of guest musicians, so the emphasis falls on the band's practice of inviting performers, not on his role.
whyWrong.C: Says only that he toured, which leaves out the keyboardist role entirely.
whyWrong.D: The "It was in 2000 that ..." construction is a cleft that puts the stress on the year; the role is mentioned but demoted to a modifier.

tips: When a stem says "emphasize X," check which part of the sentence X occupies — emphasis lives in the main clause, not in a stray adjective.

whyCorrect: The goal is to name the specific type of neutrino research, and the notes give exactly one: neutrino oscillations. Only choice C both identifies Kim and states that his known research is on oscillations, so it is the only option that satisfies the stem's requirement.

whyWrong.A: Describes neutrinos in general and never mentions Kim or any research of his.
whyWrong.B: Gives his field and nationality, which is background, not the type of research.
whyWrong.D: Says he has advanced understanding of neutrinos but stops short of naming oscillations, so the specific type is still missing.

commonMistakes: Picking a sentence that is accurate and well written without checking that it contains the one detail the stem demands.

whyCorrect: A comparison has to state how the two hypotheses relate on the same measure. The notes give that measure: Fodor counts only low-level systems as modular, while Carruthers's MMH counts all cognitive systems. Choice B puts both on that scale and says Fodor's definition is the less expansive of the two, which is the comparison the student wants.

whyWrong.A: Misreports the disagreement. Both scientists accept that the mind contains innate modules; they differ over how far modularity extends.
whyWrong.C: Contradicts the notes. Both hypotheses treat low-level systems such as perception and language as modular, so that is where they agree, not where they differ.
whyWrong.D: Only puts the two in chronological order and describes Carruthers's view; Fodor's position is never characterized, so nothing is compared.

tips: For a comparison task, make sure the sentence says something about both items on a single shared dimension.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tells you what was missing before 1917: a procedure that senators could put into use to cut off debate and force a vote. The blank therefore needs a word meaning "called upon" or "put into effect," which is what it means to invoke a rule or measure.

whyWrong.A: "Improvised" means made up on the spot, which contradicts "formal measure" — a formal rule is exactly the thing you do not invent in the moment.
whyWrong.C: "Abolished" means done away with. Abolishing a measure would not end a debate, and the sentence says no such measure existed to begin with.
whyWrong.D: "Partitioned" means divided into parts, which does nothing to stop a prolonged debate.

tips: Rules, powers, and procedures are invoked; the verb has to fit the noun it acts on.

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the evidence, and it is all positive: critics called one film "galvanizing" and the other "exuberant." "For example" marks it as an illustration of how the films are regarded now, so the blank must describe a positive reception.

whyWrong.B: "Skeptically" implies doubt, the opposite of the praise the example supplies.
whyWrong.C: "Neutrally" means without a positive or negative slant, but the quoted praise is plainly enthusiastic.
whyWrong.D: "Strangely" describes an odd manner of judging rather than a favorable one, and nothing in the example is odd.

commonMistakes: Letting the opening "Whatever the general attitude ... when they were initially released" push you toward a negative word; that clause refuses to say what the early reception was.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two styles. Realists aimed at accuracy about ordinary working people; the romantic paintings did the opposite, and the tail of the sentence tells you how — they hid every imperfection. A style that hides flaws and plays up beauty or heroism is overstating those qualities, so "exaggerate" is the word that completes the contrast.

whyWrong.B: "Correct" would mean fixing an error in the subjects' beauty or heroism, which is not something a painting does to a quality.
whyWrong.C: "Undermine" means weaken. Weakening a subject's beauty runs against "hiding all imperfection," which is flattery, not criticism.
whyWrong.D: "Mock" makes the romantic painters ridicule their subjects, but they idealized them.

tips: When a sentence sets up a contrast, use the half you already understand — here, accuracy — to fix the direction of the missing word.

whyCorrect: The blank has to explain why researchers struggle to study these cats. The earlier sentences say they live alone in out-of-the-way places like Mount Everest, so the obstacle is that their habitats sit far away from where people are. "Distant from large populations of humans" restates "out-of-the-way" in the terms the sentence needs.

whyWrong.A: "Drawn to" would put the cats near people, which would make them easier to observe, not harder.
whyWrong.B: "Full of" large human populations contradicts "live mostly alone in out-of-the-way parts of Asia."
whyWrong.D: "Responsible for" large human populations makes no sense as a property of a habitat and does nothing to explain the research difficulty.

tips: A because-clause has to supply a cause; test each option by asking whether it would actually make research hard.

whyCorrect: Everything before the last sentence is a catalog of things to look at: silvered moss hung like festoons, pungent pine cones, resplendent green, cypresses spread along the water, weeping willows. "This gorgeous display" gathers all of that into one word, so "display" means an impressive sight — a spectacle.

whyWrong.B: "Reproduction" means a copy of something else, but the scenery is the real thing, not an imitation.
whyWrong.C: "Pretentiousness" carries a sneer at false grandeur; the passage admires the landscape without any hint of criticism.
whyWrong.D: "Disguise" implies something is being concealed, and nothing in the description hides anything.

commonMistakes: Choosing a meaning the word can carry in other contexts instead of the one the surrounding sentences actually support.

whyCorrect: Track the three moves. First, historians of capitalism say little about precolonial African capitalism and so leave the impression that capitalism was imposed from outside. Second, Candido and others show features of capitalism were already there. Third, the last sentence explains the gap: those historians rely on archival longitudinal data, which precolonial Africa largely lacks. That is a misleading feature of their work, followed by an account of why it arises.

whyWrong.A: No disagreement over what counts as a feature of capitalism appears; both sides use the same features, such as private property in land.
whyWrong.C: The Africanist scholars' method is never described or judged; the method discussed is that of the historians of capitalism.
whyWrong.D: There is no debate over interpreting archival data. The point is that the archival data does not exist for much of precolonial Africa.

tips: When the final sentence begins "One reason for this," the text's purpose almost always includes explaining something, not just reporting it.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence sets up that admired figures back Crowley's writing, and the rest of the text delivers one such endorsement in detail: Bloom praises Little, Big for blending Schiller's naive and sentimental modes when Schiller treated them as alternatives. The Schiller material exists to explain what Bloom admires, so the text's job is to give the reason behind a critic's high opinion of a novel.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is said about what prompted Crowley to write anything; the focus is on how a critic responded.
whyWrong.C: Merrill is named once as a champion of Crowley's work, and none of his own writing is described, so no comparison takes place.
whyWrong.D: The text says the opposite — Little, Big shows a work can be both naive and sentimental rather than one or the other.

commonMistakes: Mistaking Schiller's two-category scheme for the text's own claim; the passage cites it only to show what Crowley's novel breaks.

whyCorrect: The text names two advantages and endorses both. Community science promotes engagement by showing the public what a scientist's day looks like, and it is effective because it multiplies the data collected, as the butterfly study shows. The main idea has to keep both benefits and treat both as real, which only one option does.

whyWrong.A: Reduces the whole text to a single study, misnames the researcher, and invents a reaction of surprise that the text never reports.
whyWrong.C: Adds a drawback about data accuracy that the text never raises; the text calls the data increase a strength.
whyWrong.D: Keeps the data benefit but denies the engagement benefit, which the text states outright.

tips: When a text lists two advantages, the main idea is the option that carries both without adding a qualification of its own.

whyCorrect: Her behavior is checking repeatedly whether the guests have gone. The text then supplies the reason: the parlor is her space for her little school, the salon leaves it out of order, and it has to become a classroom again the next morning. She is waiting on the room, not on the people in it.

whyWrong.A: Nothing indicates any opinion of the guests; the text never reports what she thinks of them or any attempt to persuade them.
whyWrong.C: The school already exists and is held in that parlor; there is no new school and no plan she wants supported.
whyWrong.D: No task elsewhere in the house is mentioned, and her concern is with the parlor itself, not with Salome's availability.

commonMistakes: Reading impatience as dislike of the guests when the passage ties it to a practical need for the room.

whyCorrect: Turn the hypothesis into a prediction first. Large vortices produce big pressure fluctuations at the snout of narrow- and intermediate-headed fish but only small ones for wide-headed fish, so if greater fluctuations mean better avoidance, intermediate-headed fish should hit large-vortex obstructions less often than wide-headed fish do. A finding that the two groups bumped into obstructions equally often removes exactly the difference the hypothesis predicts.

whyWrong.A: Gives a rate for wide-headed fish alone with nothing to compare it against, so "less than half" cannot show whether the predicted gap exists.
whyWrong.C: Wide-headed fish bumping more often than intermediate-headed fish is precisely what the hypothesis predicts, so this supports it.
whyWrong.D: Compares individuals within one head shape, which says nothing about the relationship between pressure fluctuations and avoidance across shapes.

tips: Before reading the choices, write down what the hypothesis predicts should differ; a challenge is the finding where that difference fails to appear.

whyCorrect: The student's word is "must" — IGF-1 variation is being treated as the explanation for size differences between breeds. To undermine that, you only need to show the gene is not working alone. If IGF-1 is one of several genes known to affect dog size, then the size variance cannot be attributed to IGF-1 variants by itself.

whyWrong.A: Limits the finding to dogs versus other species, but the student's claim is only about dog breeds, so this leaves it untouched.
whyWrong.C: Says most breeds carry different variants, which is consistent with the variants tracking size differences rather than against it.
whyWrong.D: States that IGF-1 variation does produce substantial size variance, which agrees with the student instead of undermining the conclusion.

commonMistakes: Looking for a statement that contradicts the study's data; here the flaw is in the student's leap to a sole cause, so the counter is any evidence of other causes.

whyCorrect: The claim is that time is conceptualized on egocentric axes — directions defined by where the speaker's own body is pointed, the way English front/back works. A group that gestures uphill for the future no matter which way the speaker is facing is using the landscape, not the body, as its reference frame. That is a non-egocentric system in a real culture, which is enough to break a claim of universality.

whyWrong.A: Shared grammatical structures say nothing about whether the spatial frame is anchored to the speaker.
whyWrong.C: Opposite directions for past and future is exactly what an egocentric front/back scheme produces, so this fits the claim rather than weakening it.
whyWrong.D: A difference in how many gestures are used is about frequency, not about which axis the gestures are organized around.

tips: To weaken a universal claim you need one genuine counterexample, so look for the option that describes a system built on a different principle, not just a different amount.

whyCorrect: Two ideas have to combine. Camacho and McLachlan say "invasive" and "native" describe temporary circumstances, and climate change can push species out of old ranges and open up new ones. Apply that to Wisconsin's label on the walnut twig beetle and the conclusion is about time: the label can be right today and stop being right later.

whyWrong.A: Invents a history in which the beetle already lived in Wisconsin and was driven out; the text never discusses the beetle's past range.
whyWrong.B: Singles out the beetle as the one case where the distinction fails now, but the text's point is that the labels are temporary in general, not that this one case is special today.
whyWrong.C: Depends on climate not changing, while the whole inference rests on climate change altering where species can live.

commonMistakes: Concluding the labels are useless; the text says they are temporary, which is a claim about durability, not validity.

whyCorrect: Malthus was an economist writing about human population outrunning food production. Darwin's fall 1838 entry ties the biological struggle for survival to that essay by labeling it "as inference from Malthus," and the notebook begun in October 1838 echoes it with "the grand crush of population." So by October 1838 at the latest, Darwin had taken an idea from economics and applied it to living species.

whyWrong.A: The text dates the notebooks to 1838 and gives 1858 only as the publication year of On the Origin of Species; nothing places any entry that late.
whyWrong.B: Reverses the direction of influence. Darwin drew on Malthus, not the other way around, and no observation of animals is credited to Malthus.
whyWrong.D: Malthus wrote about human populations and agriculture, so the biological principle was not already stated in the same terms, and no other economists are mentioned.

tips: When a text gives two dates, check whether the question hinges on which came first; here the October notebook fixes the latest possible date.

whyCorrect: Turner is one of nearly two thousand African Americans, so that noun is a plain plural. The relative clause "who won elections" describes them, and "elections" is also a plain plural — the elections do not own anything in this sentence. No apostrophe belongs anywhere in the blank.

whyWrong.A: Puts possessive apostrophes on both nouns; "Americans'" would have to own something, and it owns nothing here.
whyWrong.B: "Election's" is possessive, but the sentence never names anything belonging to an election.
whyWrong.C: "American's" is singular possessive, which clashes with "nearly two thousand" and again marks ownership that does not exist.

tips: Numbers like "two thousand" force a plural noun, so any singular possessive in the choices can go immediately.

whyCorrect: The subject is "The trailblazing accomplishments," which is plural. Everything after it — "of Goldin, winner of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Economics for her work on women in the labor force" — is prepositional and appositive material that cannot change the subject's number. A plural subject in the present tense takes "attest."

whyWrong.A: Singular verb, which agrees with "Goldin" rather than with "accomplishments."
whyWrong.C: Also singular, and the present perfect frames the attesting as completed rather than as a continuing fact.
whyWrong.D: Singular, and the progressive suggests an action currently in progress, which does not fit a general statement about what her accomplishments show.

commonMistakes: Letting the long modifier between the subject and the verb pull the verb into agreement with the nearest name.

whyCorrect: "Hungary and Ireland" identifies which of the thirty-eight member nations the two prices belong to, and "respectively" only works if those names sit tight against the figures they pair with. That makes the names an essential appositive, and an essential appositive takes no punctuation before it: "in fellow OECD nations Hungary and Ireland, respectively."

whyWrong.A: A comma turns the names into supplementary information, which reads as though the fellow OECD nations were only Hungary and Ireland when there are thirty-eight.
whyWrong.B: A colon presents what follows as a separate specification set off from the clause, again loosening a link the sentence needs to keep tight for "respectively" to work.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon has to join two independent clauses, and "Hungary and Ireland, respectively" is not a clause at all.

tips: A common noun followed directly by the names it refers to — "the poet Keats," "fellow OECD nations Hungary and Ireland" — takes no punctuation between them.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete: "The mycorrhizal association ... is well documented" and "sharing nutrients via fungal hyphae and the host tree's roots, the organisms form a kind of social system ..." Two independent clauses need a real boundary, and the dash supplies one. The colon is ruled out by the end of the same sentence, which already uses one before "a community"; two colons in a single sentence leave the reader unable to tell which one governs.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation at all runs the two clauses together.
whyWrong.B: A second colon in a sentence that already ends with "... than plants: a community" makes the structure ambiguous, even though a colon would otherwise be defensible here.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Read to the end of the sentence before choosing a colon; a mark that is fine in isolation can collide with punctuation already there.

whyCorrect: "Because" starts a clause, and a clause needs a subject and a verb. The only option that supplies both is "they're" — that is, "because they are descendants of Proto-Kru." The pronoun is plural because it stands for the thirty-eight Kru languages.

whyWrong.A: "Its" is a possessive with no verb, leaving "because its descendants of Proto-Kru" without a predicate, and it is singular besides.
whyWrong.C: "Their" is also possessive and verbless, producing the same fragment even though the number is right.
whyWrong.D: "It's" does contain a verb, but the singular "it" cannot refer to thirty-eight languages that are themselves the descendants.

tips: After "because," check first that the option gives you a subject and a verb; only then worry about which pronoun.
